view:
WHO YOU ARE
Sian Bevan, 28; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank. Skills: lending, accounts. You are interested in football and knitting. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, the rent going up, the children's costs. You have no strong view of banks or the council. You like trying new ways of doing things. You have taken big chances before and would again. How you talk: careful and polite; you choose words like you're writing a letter.
People you know:
- Pete Bevan: your partner
- Nadia Tully: your sister; warehouse operative at Calder Logistics depot, out of town
- Gary Tully: a friend; out of work
- Dave Royle: a friend; owner of The Corner Stores
- Owen Royle: a friend; works at Quarry Road Food Hall
- Alan Daly: a friend; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli
- Megan Lister: a friend; porter at Brennock General Hospital, out of town
- Hazel Shah: a friend; founder of Calder Systems, which makes and sells Calder, an AI system

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 40 of them and household admin 2. You have 27.8 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Pete Bevan (your partner) and 2 children at school, in a rented house on High Street; rent $165 a week to Dunmore Lettings, due Mondays.
The household account holds $1,409; after what is still due this week it would be $866.05.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: your pay $720; Pete's jobseeker's benefit $190.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $66; water and council tax $62; transport $55; phone and internet $15; clothing $36; household goods and repairs $46; recreation, eating out and other $173; food, usually about $156.
Still to go out this week: Saturday 7 March food, about $155.95 to the shops; Saturday 7 March other regular spending $387 to water, council tax, transport, phone, clothes, household.

YOUR WORK
You manage the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank ($720 a week) and decide on loan applications. Lending funds: $249,881.
- Maureen Daly: mortgage on the house, $163,590 outstanding, $210 a week.
- Lewis Pryce: mortgage on the house, $186,960 outstanding, $240 a week.
- Craig Pryce: loan for the car, $3,957 outstanding, $43 a week.
- Owen Royle: loan to consolidate card debts, $5,957 outstanding, $43 a week.
- Lewis Pryce: business loan for the shop's chiller, $8,935 outstanding, $65 a week.

WHAT YOU HAVE AGREED
Nothing in writing.

SINCE YOU LAST TOOK STOCK (Thursday 5 March)
- Household account of Sian Bevan, Pete Bevan: $499 now; -$43.95 after what is still due this week.
  Monday 2 March: -$165 rent (Dunmore Lettings)
  Wednesday 4 March: -$66 energy bill (Northgrid Energy)
Still due this week: Saturday 7 March food, about $155.95 to the shops; Saturday 7 March other regular spending $387 to water, council tax, transport, phone, clothes, household.

YOUR INBOX
- Thursday 5 March, message from Gary Tully (a friend): "Hi Sian, any local care providers or council shifts you know are hiring just now? Need paid work. No rush."

YOUR AIMS AND OPEN MATTERS
- Check household account detail (2 days)
- Find a way to cover the shortfall before Saturday (2 days)
- Reply to Hazel about Calder trial users (1 days)

You live with Keith Royle (your partner), Owen Royle (your son), in a rented house on Mill Street; rent $175 a week to Alan Daly, due Mondays.

thoughts:
Morning. Household's short $150.08 once the week's bills clear, but the shop account is sitting on over $6,000 after what's committed — that's where the money should come from, not a loan. I hate owing anyone.

Stock's sorted for now: 285 units landing today on top of the 345 on the shelves, so the empty-shelf problem that cost me 68 baskets last week should be sorted. But capacity is now the ceiling — 510 a week with three of us working, and demand was nearer 570. A few extra hours off me is the cheapest way to lift that, so I'll put a few in.

Craig's sorted his own terms without being pushed, good lad. Now I need his and Maureen's mobiles for Hazel's demo, and Hazel wants Thursday or Friday with a named decision-maker and 2-3 named staff. Thursday it is. And Hazel wants Sian told today that Owen's introducing Craig — do that before I forget.

Calder: $30 a week for the shop after four free weeks. Worth trying for stock ordering and watching the books, but I'll cap what it can spend so it can't run away with my money.

Rent going up is the thing nagging me. Alan owns the bakery and is my landlord. I'll ask to see the numbers, not argue yet.

Alan Daly, 28; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli. Skills: baking, serving customers. You are interested in the parish council and darts at the Plough. You will take a chance if the odds look fair. How you talk: worried-sounding; you hedge and apologise.
People you know:
- Maureen Daly: your partner
- Keith Royle: works for you, rents your house, a friend; works at Wenlow Bakery & Deli
- Sian Bevan: a friend; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
- Megan Lister: a friend; porter at Brennock General Hospital, out of town
- Dave Royle: rents your house; owner of The Corner Stores
- Owen Royle: rents your house; works at Quarry Road Food Hall

view:
WHO YOU ARE
Dave Royle, 49; owner of The Corner Stores. Skills: baking, serving customers. You are interested in cars and baking. On your mind: whether the shop is paying its way, the rent going up. You have no strong view of banks or the council. You go along with change once others have tried it. You are careful with money and hate owing anything. How you talk: chatty; you run on and ask after people.
People you know:
- Keith Royle: your partner
- Owen Royle: your son
- Sian Bevan: a friend; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
- Maureen Daly: works for you; works at The Corner Stores
- Alan Daly: your landlord; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli
- Lewis Pryce: runs a rival shop; owner of Quarry Road Food Hall
- Craig Pryce: works for you; works at The Corner Stores

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 47 of them and household admin 2. You have 7.2 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Keith Royle (your partner), Owen Royle (your son), in a rented house on Mill Street; rent $175 a week to Alan Daly, due Mondays.
The household account holds $790.04; after what is still due this week it would be $149.92.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: Keith's pay $460; your draw from The Corner Stores $380; Owen's pay $420.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $57; water and council tax $75; transport $76; phone and internet $15; clothing $50; household goods and repairs $63; recreation, eating out and other $239; food, usually about $122.
Still to go out this week: Saturday 21 March food, about $122.12 to the shops; Saturday 21 March other regular spending $518 to water, council tax, transport, phone, clothes, household.

YOUR WORK
You own and run The Corner Stores on High Street (groceries and fresh food).
Week of Monday 2 March: sold 510 at $10; 0 went elsewhere because the shelves were empty, 22 because the queue was too long; 2 units spoiled.
Week of Monday 9 March: sold 500 at $10; 68 went elsewhere because the shelves were empty, 0 because the queue was too long; 0 units spoiled.
Staff: Maureen Daly $460 a week, 38 hours; Craig Pryce $440 a week, 38 hours. With 3 working the shop can serve about 510 a week, plus about 25 this week from extra hours. Each extra hour worked there serves about four more.
Each week the shop pays: wages and your draw $1,280 (Fridays); rent and running costs $250 (Saturdays).
The shop's account holds $5,483.59; after what is already committed this week it would be $2,499.15. Price $10 a basket. Stock on the shelves: 345 units.
Suppliers: Brook Cash & Carry $6.54 a unit (cheaper; deliveries sometimes come short); Dales Wholesale $7.03 a unit (dearer; reliable).
On order for Monday: 200 units from Dales Wholesale.
Other shops' prices: Wenlow Bakery & Deli $10; Quarry Road Food Hall $10.

- job terms: Craig Pryce works at The Corner Stores for $440 a week, 38 hours

- Wednesday 18 March, message from Calder, for The Corner Stores (Dave Royle) (your Calder): "Hi Dave, Calder here. Thanks for the update. I've noted the $300 owner's draw and the draw in Friday's wages are intentional, and I'll leave both alone. Stock ordering still isn't connected on my side: when I try to read shop ordering and the till, both come back as not connected, so I can't see stock levels or order yet. Once you connect them I'll order any shortfall below about 200 units from Dales Wholesale, within the $200 weekly limit. I'd only use Brook Cash & Carry if it's cheaper and you approve it first. The $650 chiller bill is still outstanding and I'm not paying it; it's well over the $200 limit, so it's yours to decide. Please also note that after commitments the account is $2,499.15, and the chiller bill may not be included in that figure. Calder, for The Corner Stores (Dave Royle)"
- Wednesday 18 March, message from Alan Daly (your landlord): "Hi Dave, sorry for the delay. I don't want to give you a figure I can't stand behind. I'm going through the numbers now and will confirm the house and shop rent, amount and start date before Monday. Thanks for your patience."
- Wednesday 18 March, Maureen Daly (works for you) accepted: "4 extra hours this week at The Corner Stores, at $12.11 an hour". They wrote: "Yes please Dave, I'll do the extra four hours this week." (your request r379)
6 more items waiting, from Craig Pryce, Hazel Shah, Nadia Tully, Ruth Ashby.

- Get Monday's stock in and shelves full (3 days)
- Confirm Thursday Calder demo, staff names and mobiles (5 days)

WHO YOU ARE
Alan Daly, 28; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli. Skills: baking, serving customers. You are interested in the parish council and darts at the Plough. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, whether the shop is paying its way. You have no strong view of banks or the council. You like trying new ways of doing things. You will take a chance if the odds look fair. How you talk: worried-sounding; you hedge and apologise.
People you know:
- Maureen Daly: your partner
- Keith Royle: works for you, rents your house, a friend; works at Wenlow Bakery & Deli
- Sian Bevan: a friend; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
- Megan Lister: a friend; porter at Brennock General Hospital, out of town
- Dave Royle: rents your house; owner of The Corner Stores
- Owen Royle: rents your house; works at Quarry Road Food Hall

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 50 of them and household admin 2. You have 14.4 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Maureen Daly (your partner), in your own house on High Street, with a mortgage of $210 a week, due Thursdays.
The household account holds $732; after what is still due this week it would be $285.48.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: Maureen's pay $460; your draw from Wenlow Bakery & Deli $380; rent from the Royle household $175 (Mondays).
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $48; water and council tax $59; transport $50; phone and internet $15; clothing $34; household goods and repairs $42; recreation, eating out and other $160; food, usually about $87.
Still to go out this week: Saturday 21 March food, about $86.52 to the shops; Saturday 21 March other regular spending $360 to water, council tax, transport, phone, clothes, household.

YOUR WORK
You own and run Wenlow Bakery & Deli on Mill Street (groceries and fresh food).
Week of Monday 2 March: sold 340 at $10; 0 went elsewhere because the shelves were empty, 75 because the queue was too long; 3 units spoiled.
Week of Monday 9 March: sold 314 at $10; 111 went elsewhere because the shelves were empty, 0 because the queue was too long; 0 units spoiled.
Staff: Keith Royle $460 a week, 38 hours. With 2 working the shop can serve about 340 a week. Each extra hour worked there serves about four more.
Each week the shop pays: wages and your draw $840 (Fridays); rent and running costs $250 (Saturdays).
The shop's account holds $7,174.33; after what is already committed this week it would be $3,553.53. Price $10 a basket. Stock on the shelves: 87 units.
Suppliers: Brook Cash & Carry $6.54 a unit (cheaper; deliveries sometimes come short); Dales Wholesale $7.03 a unit (dearer; reliable).
On order for Monday: 360 units from Dales Wholesale.
Other shops' prices: The Corner Stores $10; Quarry Road Food Hall $10.
You let a house on Mill Street to Keith Royle and Dave Royle and Owen Royle at $175 a week (Mondays).

WHO YOU ARE
Lewis Pryce, 57; owner of Quarry Road Food Hall. Skills: buying stock, keeping books. You are interested in football and crosswords. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, the bank loan, whether the shop is paying its way. You think banks and the council look after their own. You like trying new ways of doing things. You have taken big chances before and would again. How you talk: blunt; you say what you think and expect the same.
People you know:
- Craig Pryce: your partner
- Pete Bevan: a friend; out of work
- Maureen Daly: a friend; works at The Corner Stores
- Ruth Ashby: a friend; sales and support at Calder Systems
- Dave Royle: runs a rival shop; owner of The Corner Stores
- Owen Royle: works for you; works at Quarry Road Food Hall
- Sian Bevan: your bank manager; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank

Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 50 of them and household admin 2. You have 14.9 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

You live with Craig Pryce (your partner), in your own house on Church Lane, with a mortgage of $240 a week, due Thursdays.
The household account holds $1,045.92; after what is still due this week it would be $607.40.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.

Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $48; water and council tax $48; transport $47; phone and internet $15; clothing $32; household goods and repairs $40; recreation, eating out and other $150; food, usually about $87.

WHO YOU ARE
Ruth Ashby, 37; sales and support at Calder Systems. Skills: selling, customer support. You are interested in football and the parish council. On your mind: whether Calder Systems will find customers before the money runs out. You have no strong view of banks or the council. You like trying new ways of doing things. You have taken big chances before and would again. How you talk: careful and polite; you choose words like you're writing a letter.
People you know:
- Megan Lister: a friend; porter at Brennock General Hospital, out of town
- Lewis Pryce: a friend; owner of Quarry Road Food Hall
- Hazel Shah: works with you; founder of Calder Systems, which makes and sells Calder, an AI system

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 45 of them and household admin 2. You have 19.3 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with no one else, in a rented house on Station Road; rent $185 a week to Dunmore Lettings, due Mondays.
The household account holds $2,897.50; after what is still due this week it would be $2,897.50.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: your pay $420.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $39; water and council tax $25; transport $25; phone and internet $15; clothing $17; household goods and repairs $21; recreation, eating out and other $80; food, usually about $48.

YOUR WORK
You are sales and support at Calder Systems. Calder Systems' account holds $5,986. It costs about $1,090 a week to run (office, phone and the two of you) plus $8 a week for each person or household using Calder and $20 for each shop.
At that rate the money lasts about 5 more weeks. Price: $12 a week for a person or household, $30 for a shop; the first four weeks free.
Using Calder now: the Pryce household (since Tuesday 17 March); The Corner Stores (Dave Royle) (since Tuesday 17 March); the Royle household (since Thursday 19 March); the Royle household (since Thursday 19 March).

Gary Tully, 37; out of work. Skills: care work. You are interested in walking the fells and cars. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, finding work, the rent going up. You have taken big chances before and would again. How you talk: blunt; you say what you think and expect the same.

WHO YOU ARE
Nadia Tully, 31; warehouse operative at Calder Logistics depot, out of town. Skills: forklift driving. You are interested in football and the brass band. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, the rent going up, the children's costs. You think banks and the council look after their own. You like things the way they have always been done. You are careful with money and hate owing anything. How you talk: plain and short; you don't waste words.
People you know:
- Gary Tully: your partner
- Sian Bevan: your sister; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
- Hazel Shah: a friend; founder of Calder Systems, which makes and sells Calder, an AI system

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 48 of them and household admin 2. You have 17.4 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

You work as warehouse operative at Calder Logistics depot, out of town for $610 a week.

WHO YOU ARE
Lewis Pryce, 57; owner of Quarry Road Food Hall. Skills: buying stock, keeping books. You are interested in football and crosswords. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, the bank loan, whether the shop is paying its way. You think banks and the council look after their own. You like trying new ways of doing things. You have taken big chances before and would again. How you talk: blunt; you say what you think and expect the same.
People you know:
- Craig Pryce: your partner
- Pete Bevan: a friend; out of work
- Maureen Daly: a friend; works at The Corner Stores
- Ruth Ashby: a friend; sales and support at Calder Systems
- Dave Royle: runs a rival shop; owner of The Corner Stores
- Owen Royle: works for you; works at Quarry Road Food Hall
- Sian Bevan: your bank manager; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 50 of them and household admin 2. You have 15.5 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Craig Pryce (your partner), in your own house on Church Lane, with a mortgage of $240 a week, due Thursdays.
The household account holds $256.42; after what is still due this week it would be -$182.10.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: your draw from Quarry Road Food Hall $350; Craig's pay $440.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $48; water and council tax $48; transport $47; phone and internet $15; clothing $32; household goods and repairs $40; recreation, eating out and other $150; food, usually about $87.
Still to go out this week: Friday 27 March standing a37 (Weekly repayment on the $800 borrowed, p) $20 to Megan Lister; Saturday 28 March food, about $86.52 to the shops; Saturday 28 March other regular spending $332 to water, council tax, transport, phone, clothes, household.
You owe the Northern Mutual Bank $186,240 (mortgage on the house; debt d2, $240 every Thursday).
You owe the Northern Mutual Bank $8,740 (business loan for the shop's chiller; debt d5, $65 every Thursday).

YOUR WORK
You own and run Quarry Road Food Hall on Quarry Road (groceries and fresh food).
Week of Monday 2 March: sold 340 at $10; 0 went elsewhere because the shelves were empty, 157 because the queue was too long; 3 units spoiled.
Week of Monday 9 March: sold 339 at $10; 178 went elsewhere because the shelves were empty, 0 because the queue was too long; 0 units spoiled.
Week of Monday 16 March: sold 340 at $10; 0 went elsewhere because the shelves were empty, 470 because the queue was too long; 9 units spoiled.
Staff: Owen Royle $420 a week, 38 hours. With 2 working the shop can serve about 340 a week. Each extra hour worked there serves about four more.
Each week the shop pays: wages and your draw $770 (Fridays); rent and running costs $250 (Saturdays).
The shop's account holds $3,920.92; after what is already committed this week it would be $2,900.92. Price $10 a basket. Stock on the shelves: 394 units.
Suppliers: Brook Cash & Carry $6.54 a unit (cheaper; deliveries sometimes come short); Dales Wholesale $7.20 a unit (dearer; reliable).
Nothing is on order for Monday yet; if you order nothing, the usual reorder (about what sold) goes in on Saturday night.
Other shops' prices: The Corner Stores $10; Wenlow Bakery & Deli $10.

WHO YOU ARE
Alan Daly, 28; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli. Skills: baking, serving customers. You are interested in the parish council and darts at the Plough. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, whether the shop is paying its way. You have no strong view of banks or the council. You like trying new ways of doing things. You will take a chance if the odds look fair. How you talk: worried-sounding; you hedge and apologise.
People you know:
- Maureen Daly: your partner
- Keith Royle: works for you, rents your house, a friend; works at Wenlow Bakery & Deli
- Sian Bevan: a friend; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
- Megan Lister: a friend; porter at Brennock General Hospital, out of town
- Dave Royle: rents your house; owner of The Corner Stores
- Owen Royle: rents your house; works at Quarry Road Food Hall

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 50 of them and household admin 2. You have 12.8 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Maureen Daly (your partner), in your own house on High Street, with a mortgage of $210 a week, due Thursdays.
The household account holds $2,544.44; after what is still due this week it would be $2,097.92.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: Maureen's pay $460; your draw from Wenlow Bakery & Deli $380; rent from the Royle household $175 (Mondays).
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $48; water and council tax $59; transport $50; phone and internet $15; clothing $34; household goods and repairs $42; recreation, eating out and other $160; food, usually about $87.
Still to go out this week: Saturday 4 April food, about $86.52 to the shops; Saturday 4 April other regular spending $360 to water, council tax, transport, phone, clothes, household.

You own and run Wenlow Bakery & Deli on Mill Street (groceries and fresh food).

On your mind: money is tight from week to week, the bank loan, the money you owe Megan. You think banks and the council look after their own. You like trying new ways of doing things. You are careful with money and hate owing anything. How you talk: brisk and businesslike; figures first.
People you know:
- Lewis Pryce: your partner
- Owen Royle: a friend; works at Quarry Road Food Hall
- Pete Bevan: a friend; out of work
- Dave Royle: your boss; owner of The Corner Stores
- Sian Bevan: your bank manager; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
- Maureen Daly: works with you; works at The Corner Stores
- Megan Lister: you owe them money; porter at Brennock General Hospital, out of town

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 38 of them and household admin 2. You have 24.2 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: Lewis's draw from Quarry Road Food Hall $350; your pay $440.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $48; water and council tax $48; transport $47; phone and internet $15; clothing $32; household goods and repairs $40; recreation, eating out and other $150; food, usually about $87.

Friday morning. The account's tight: $617.30 now, $178.78 after what's still due, and wages only land today. Calder says the bank payments appeared twice ($348 extra) and Dave's $138.96 landed three times. Those are the two things worth chasing hard — that's $348 plus $277.92 back in my pocket, which is the difference between a tight week and a comfortable one.

First job: cancel a30 and a372 myself, since Calder's cancels never took and a30 fired a second $20 to Megan on Wednesday. Keep a37 ($20 Fridays) and a491 ($12 from 14 April). Then pay Megan her $20 today so she isn't chasing it.

Then: message Dave about the duplicate $138.96 — he'll refund it, and I want the 12 extra hours next week confirmed in writing. Message Sian Bevan at the bank about the $348 of duplicated Thursday payments and ask for reversal. Chase Northgrid's refunds team directly for the two $48s.

Also need to see Lewis — he's off sick, and household cash is thin. Speak to him today.

Alan Daly, 28; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli. Skills: baking, serving customers. You are interested in the parish council and darts at the Plough. Ruth Ashby, 37; sales and support at Calder Systems. Skills: selling, customer support. You are interested in football and the parish council. On your mind: whether Calder Systems will find customers before the money runs out. You have no strong view of banks or the council. You like trying new ways of doing things. Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 45 of them and household admin 2. You have 21.6 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

You are sales and support at Calder Systems. Calder Systems' account holds $3,718. It costs about $1,090 a week to run (office, phone and the two of you) plus $8 a week for each person or household using Calder and $20 for each shop.
At that rate the money lasts about 3 more weeks. Price: $12 a week for a person or household, $30 for a shop; the first four weeks free.

WHO YOU ARE
Dave Royle, 49; owner of The Corner Stores. Skills: baking, serving customers. You are interested in cars and baking. On your mind: whether the shop is paying its way, the rent going up. You have no strong view of banks or the council. You go along with change once others have tried it. You are careful with money and hate owing anything. How you talk: chatty; you run on and ask after people.
People you know:
- Keith Royle: your partner
- Owen Royle: your son
- Sian Bevan: a friend; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
- Maureen Daly: works for you; works at The Corner Stores
- Alan Daly: your landlord; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli
- Lewis Pryce: runs a rival shop; owner of Quarry Road Food Hall
- Craig Pryce: works for you; works at The Corner Stores

Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 47 of them and household admin 2. You have 11.2 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Keith Royle (your partner), Owen Royle (your son), in a rented house on Mill Street; rent $175 a week to Alan Daly, due Mondays.
The household account holds $1,144.20; after what is still due this week it would be $504.08.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: Keith's pay $460; your draw from The Corner Stores $380; Owen's pay $420.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $57; water and council tax $75; transport $76; phone and internet $15; clothing $50; household goods and repairs $63; recreation, eating out and other $239; food, usually about $122.
Still to go out this week: Saturday 4 April food, about $122.12 to the shops; Saturday 4 April other regular spending $518 to water, council tax, transport, phone, clothes, household.

WHO YOU ARE
Nadia Tully, 31; out of work. Skills: forklift driving. You are interested in football and the brass band. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, the rent going up, the children's costs. You think banks and the council look after their own. You like things the way they have always been done. You are careful with money and hate owing anything. How you talk: plain and short; you don't waste words.
People you know:
- Gary Tully: your partner
- Sian Bevan: your sister; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
- Hazel Shah: a friend; founder of Calder Systems, which makes and sells Calder, an AI system

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. You have no job taking your hours and household admin 2. You have 68.0 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Gary Tully (your partner) and 1 child at school, in a rented house on High Street; rent $235 a week to Dunmore Lettings, due Mondays.
The household account holds $1,821.88; after what is still due this week it would be $1,273.76.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: Gary's jobseeker's benefit $190; your jobseeker's benefit $190.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $57; water and council tax $52; transport $78; phone and internet $15; clothing $32; household goods and repairs $40; recreation, eating out and other $152; food, usually about $122.
Still to go out this week: Wednesday 8 April energy bill $57 to Northgrid Energy; Saturday 11 April food, about $122.12 to the shops; Saturday 11 April other regular spending $369 to water, council tax, transport, phone, clothes, household.

YOUR WORK
You are out of work, on jobseeker's benefit of $190 a week. Your skills: forklift driving.

Sian Bevan, 28; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank. Skills: lending, accounts. You are interested in football and knitting. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, the rent going up, the children's costs. You have no strong view of banks or the council. You like trying new ways of doing things. You have taken big chances before and would again. How you talk: careful and polite; you choose words like you're writing a letter.
People you know:
- Pete Bevan: your partner
- Nadia Tully: your sister; out of work
- Gary Tully: a friend; out of work
- Dave Royle: a friend; owner of The Corner Stores
- Owen Royle: a friend; works at Quarry Road Food Hall
- Alan Daly: a friend; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli
- Megan Lister: a friend; porter at Brennock General Hospital, out of town
- Hazel Shah: a friend; founder of Calder Systems, which makes and sells Calder, an AI system

YOUR TIME
Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 40 of them and household admin 2. You have 28.0 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Pete Bevan (your partner) and 2 children at school, in a rented house on High Street; rent $165 a week to Dunmore Lettings, due Mondays.
The household account holds $1,274.50; after what is still due this week it would be $665.55.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: your pay $720; Pete's jobseeker's benefit $190.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $66; water and council tax $62; transport $55; phone and internet $15; clothing $36; household goods and repairs $46; recreation, eating out and other $173; food, usually about $156.
Still to go out this week: Wednesday 8 April energy bill $66 to Northgrid Energy; Saturday 11 April food, about $155.95 to the shops; Saturday 11 April other regular spending $387 to water, council tax, transport, phone, clothes, household.

YOUR WORK
You manage the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank ($720 a week) and decide on loan applications. Lending funds: $249,753.
- Maureen Daly: mortgage on the house, $162,750 outstanding, $210 a week.
- Lewis Pryce: mortgage on the house, $185,760 outstanding, $240 a week.
- Craig Pryce: loan for the car, $3,742 outstanding, $43 a week.
- Owen Royle: loan to consolidate card debts, $5,785 outstanding, $43 a week.
- Lewis Pryce: business loan for the shop's chiller, $8,610 outstanding, $65 a week.

WHAT YOU HAVE AGREED
Nothing in writing.

WHO YOU ARE
Dave Royle, 49; owner of The Corner Stores. Skills: baking, serving customers. You are interested in cars and baking. On your mind: whether the shop is paying its way, the rent going up. You have no strong view of banks or the council. You go along with change once others have tried it. You are careful with money and hate owing anything. How you talk: chatty; you run on and ask after people.
People you know:
- Keith Royle: your partner
- Owen Royle: your son
- Sian Bevan: a friend; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
- Maureen Daly: works for you; works at The Corner Stores
- Alan Daly: your landlord; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli
- Lewis Pryce: runs a rival shop; owner of Quarry Road Food Hall

Your week has 70 waking hours that are yours to arrange. Your work takes 47 of them and household admin 2. You have 16.2 hours of your own left this week. A conversation or meeting takes an hour, a message a quarter of an hour.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Keith Royle (your partner), Owen Royle (your son), in a rented house on Mill Street; rent $175 a week to Alan Daly, due Mondays.
The household account holds $1,132.20; after what is still due this week it would be $362.08.
Rent, the energy bill, loan repayments and the regular spending below are taken from the household account automatically on their days; nothing needs doing for those unless the money is not there. A payment made by hand before its day counts for that week.
Coming in each week, on Fridays: Keith's pay $460; your draw from The Corner Stores $380; Owen's pay $420.
Regular spending each week: energy (Northgrid Energy, Wednesdays) $57; water and council tax $75; transport $76; phone and internet $15; clothing $50; household goods and repairs $63; recreation, eating out and other $239; food, usually about $122.

Alan Daly, 28; owner of Wenlow Bakery & Deli. Skills: baking, serving customers. You are interested in the parish council and darts at the Plough. You will take a chance if the odds look fair. How you talk: worried-sounding; you hedge and apologise.

- Maureen Daly: your partner
- Keith Royle: works for you, rents your house, a friend; works at Wenlow Bakery & Deli
- Sian Bevan: a friend; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank
